claim: Endoglycan is a member of the CD34 family of sialomucins.
source: Endoglycan is a member of the CD34 family of sialomucins (Nielsen and McNagny, 2008; Sassetti et al., 2000; Furness and McNagny, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Nielsen and McNagny, 2008; Sassetti et al., 2000; Furness and McNagny, 2006).

claim: CD34 family members are single-pass transmembrane proteins with highly conserved transmembrane and cytoplasmic domains.
source: They are single-pass transmembrane proteins with highly conserved transmembrane and cytoplasmic domains.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about CD34 family members and is referenced in the context of the manuscript.

claim: A C-terminal PDZ recognition site is found in all three CD34 family members.
source: A C-terminal PDZ recognition site is found in all three family members (Furness and McNagny, 2006; Nielsen and McNagny, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Furness and McNagny, 2006; Nielsen and McNagny, 2008).

claim: The hallmark of sialomucins is their bulky extracellular domain that is negatively charged due to extensive N- and O-glycosylation.
source: The hallmark of sialomucins is their bulky extracellular domain that is negatively charged due to extensive N- and O-glycosylation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about sialomucins and their structural features.

claim: CD34 was identified more than 20 years ago.
source: Despite the fact that CD34 was identified more than 20 years ago, very little is known about its function.
evidence: The claim is based on historical knowledge about the discovery of CD34.

claim: CD34 has been widely used as a marker for hematopoietic stem cells and precursors.
source: It has been widely used as a marker for hematopoietic stem cells and precursors.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the use of CD34 as a marker.

claim: Podocalyxin is expressed on hematopoietic stem and precursor cells.
source: Similarly, Podocalyxin is expressed on hematopoietic stem and precursor cells.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Podocalyxin expression.

claim: Podocalyxin was found in podocytes of the developing kidney.
source: In contrast to CD34, Podocalyxin was found in podocytes of the developing kidney (Kerjaschki et al., 1984; Doyonnas et al., 2005; Furness and McNagny, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kerjaschki et al., 1984; Doyonnas et al., 2005; Furness and McNagny, 2006).

claim: In the absence of Podocalyxin, podocytes do not differentiate, resulting in kidney failure and perinatal lethality in mice.
source: In the absence of Podocalyxin, podocytes do not differentiate, resulting in kidney failure and thus perinatal lethality in mice (Doyonnas et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Doyonnas et al., 2001).

claim: Podocalyxin, but not CD34, is expressed widely in the developing and mature mouse brain.
source: Podocalyxin, but not CD34, is expressed widely in the developing and mature mouse brain (Vitureira et al., 2005; Vitureira et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Vitureira et al., 2005; Vitureira et al., 2010).

claim: Podocalyxin was shown to induce microvilli and regulate cell-cell adhesion via its binding to the NHERF family of adaptor proteins that link Podocalyxin to the actin cytoskeleton.
source: Podocalyxin was shown to induce microvilli and regulate cell-cell adhesion via its binding to the NHERF (Na+/H+ exchanger regulatory factor) family of adaptor proteins that link Podocalyxin to the actin cytoskeleton (Nielsen et al., 2007; Nielsen and McNagny, 2008; Nielsen and McNagny, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Nielsen et al., 2007; Nielsen and McNagny, 2008; Nielsen and McNagny, 2009).

claim: Endoglycan is expressed in the brain and in the kidney.
source: Like Podocalyxin, Endoglycan is expressed in the brain and in the kidney.
evidence: The claim is based on the comparison with Podocalyxin and is stated in the manuscript.

claim: Only low levels of Endoglycan were found in hematopoietic tissues.
source: Only low levels were found in hematopoietic tissues (Sassetti et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Sassetti et al., 2000).

claim: Nothing is known about the function of Endoglycan prior to this study.
source: To date, nothing is known about the function of Endoglycan.
evidence: The claim is based on the state of knowledge at the time of the study.

claim: In the absence of Endoglycan, commissural axons failed to turn rostrally upon floor-plate exit.
source: In the absence of Endoglycan, commissural axons failed to turn rostrally upon floor-plate exit.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including DiI tracing experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Commissural axons were occasionally observed to turn already inside the floor-plate area in the absence of Endoglycan.
source: Occasionally, they were observed to turn already inside the floor-plate area.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including DiI tracing experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The trajectory of commissural axons in the midline area was tortuous in embryos lacking Endoglycan, but straight in control embryos.
source: Furthermore, the trajectory of commissural axons in the midline area was tortuous in embryos lacking Endoglycan, but straight in control embryos.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including DiI tracing experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Live imaging data of dI1 axons crossing the floor plate confirmed changes in axon – floor plate interaction.
source: Live imaging data of dI1 axons crossing the floor plate confirmed changes in axon – floor plate interaction.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from live imaging experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Axons were growing more slowly after silencing Endoglycan.
source: In addition, axons were growing more slowly after silencing Endoglycan and faster after overexpression of Endoglycan.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from live imaging experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Axons were growing faster after overexpression of Endoglycan.
source: In addition, axons were growing more slowly after silencing Endoglycan and faster after overexpression of Endoglycan.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from live imaging experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: In vitro assays confirmed a lower adhesive strength of growth cones to a layer of HEK cells expressing Endoglycan.
source: In vitro assays confirmed a lower adhesive strength of growth cones to a layer of HEK cells expressing Endoglycan.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro adhesion assays presented in the manuscript, including Figure 5 and Figure 6.

claim: Adhesion between growth cones overexpressing Endoglycan and control HEK cells was reduced.
source: Similarly, adhesion between growth cones overexpressing Endoglycan and control HEK cells was reduced, in agreement with a model suggesting that Endoglycan acts as a negative regulator of cell-cell adhesion during axon guidance.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro adhesion assays presented in the manuscript, including Figure 6.

claim: Endoglycan acts as a negative regulator of cell-cell adhesion during axon guidance.
source: Taken together, our in vivo and in vitro results support the hypothesis that Endoglycan acts as a negative regulator of cell-cell adhesion in commissural axon guidance.
evidence: The claim is supported by a combination of in vivo and in vitro experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Endoglycan was identified in a subtractive hybridization screen for differentially expressed floor-plate genes.
source: In a subtractive hybridization screen, we identified differentially expressed floor-plate genes as candidate guidance cues directing axons from dorsolateral commissural neurons (dI1 neurons) along the longitudinal axis after midline crossing (Bourikas et al., 2005; see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the experimental method used to identify Endoglycan.

claim: Endoglycan interfered with the correct rostral turning of commissural axons after midline crossing.
source: One of these candidates that interfered with the correct rostral turning of commissural axons after midline crossing turned out to be Endoglycan, a member of the CD34 family of sialomucins.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in ovo RNAi experiments.

claim: The conservation between species orthologues of CD34, Endoglycan and Podocalyxin is in the range of 80%, except for the mucin-like domain at the N-terminus where it drops below 40%.
source: With the exception of the mucin-like domain at the N-terminus, the conservation between species orthologues of CD34, Endoglycan and Podocalyxin is in the range of 80%, but drops below 40% within the mucin domain.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Homologies of CD34, Endoglycan and Podocalyxin within the same species are generally only in the range of 40%.
source: Homologies of these paralogous proteins within the same species are generally only in the range of 40% (Figure 1), demonstrating that, while they might share a similar overall structure, the structure can be built by quite diverse primary amino acid sequences.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Endoglycan was expressed mainly in the nervous system during development, as levels in non-neuronal tissues were much lower.
source: Endoglycan was expressed mainly in the nervous system during development, as levels in non-neuronal tissues were much lower (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the neural tube, Endoglycan was expressed ubiquitously, including floor-plate cells at HH21.
source: In the neural tube, Endoglycan was expressed ubiquitously, including floor-plate cells at HH21 (Hamburger and Hamilton stage 21; Hamburger and Hamilton, 1951; Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: By HH25, Endoglycan expression was still found throughout the neural tube with higher levels detected in dorsal neurons (including dI1 neurons) and motoneurons.
source: By HH25, expression was still found throughout the neural tube with higher levels detected in dorsal neurons (including dI1 neurons) and motoneurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Endoglycan expression was maintained in the floor plate at HH25.
source: Endoglycan expression was also maintained in the floor plate (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Downregulation of Endoglycan with dsRNA derived from the ORF resulted in 61.7 ± 6.4% injection sites with aberrant axon guidance.
source: Downregulation of Endoglycan with dsRNA derived from the ORF resulted in 61.7 ± 6.4% injection sites with aberrant axon guidance.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of DiI tracing experiments shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Aberrant axonal pathfinding was seen at 82.3 ± 5.6% of the injection sites with dsRNA derived from the 3'UTR of Endoglycan.
source: The effect on axon guidance was also seen with dsRNA derived from the 3'UTR, with 82.3 ± 5.6% of the injection sites with aberrant axon guidance (Figure 2L).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of DiI tracing experiments shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Aberrant axonal pathfinding was seen only at 6.7 ± 3.4% of the injection sites in untreated control embryos.
source: In contrast, aberrant axonal pathfinding was seen only at 6.7 ± 3.4% of the injection sites in untreated control embryos.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of DiI tracing experiments shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Aberrant axonal pathfinding was seen at 16.2 ± 6.0% of the injection sites for EGFP-expressing control embryos.
source: Values were 16.2 ± 6.0 for EGFP-expressing control embryos, 24.6 ± 5.8% for embryos transfected with dsRNA derived from CD34, and 23.3 ± 3.9% for embryos transfected with dsRNA derived from Podocalyxin.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of DiI tracing experiments shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Silencing CD34 did not interfere with correct navigation of axons at the midline.
source: Thus, silencing either CD34 or Podocalyxin did not interfere with correct navigation of axons at the midline.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of DiI tracing experiments shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Silencing Podocalyxin did not interfere with correct navigation of axons at the midline.
source: Thus, silencing either CD34 or Podocalyxin did not interfere with correct navigation of axons at the midline.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of DiI tracing experiments shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Floor-plate cells were aligned to form the characteristic triangular shape of the floor plate in untreated and control-treated embryos.
source: In untreated (Figure 3A–C) and control-treated embryos (Figure 3D–F), HNF3β/FoxA2-positive cells were aligned to form the characteristic triangular shape of the floor plate.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A-F.

claim: Floor-plate cells were no longer aligned to form a smooth ventral border in embryos lacking Endoglycan.
source: In contrast, floor-plate cells were no longer aligned to form a smooth ventral border in embryos lacking Endoglycan after electroporation of dsEndo into one half of the spinal cord (Figure 3G,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3G,J.

claim: Floor-plate cells were found dislocated into the commissure in embryos lacking Endoglycan.
source: On the one hand, floor-plate cells were found dislocated into the commissure formed by the Contactin2-positive axons (arrowheads in Figure 3I,L).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3I,L.

claim: The floor plate appeared to have gaps in embryos lacking Endoglycan.
source: On the other hand, the floor plate appeared to have gaps in embryos lacking Endoglycan.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The floor-plate width was significantly narrower in embryos lacking Endoglycan in comparison to age-matched controls.
source: In addition, the floor-plate width was significantly narrower in embryos lacking Endoglycan in comparison to age-matched controls (Figure 3S,T).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3T.

claim: Changes in floor-plate morphology were not due to differences in cell differentiation or patterning.
source: These changes in floor-plate morphology were not due to differences in cell differentiation or patterning (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cell death can be excluded as a contributor to the changes in the floor plate, as no Cleaved Caspase-3-positive floor-plate cells were found in any of the conditions.
source: Furthermore, we can exclude cell death as a contributor to the changes in the floor plate, as we found no Cleaved Caspase-3-positive floor-plate cells in any of the conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The shape of the floor plate was not different between control and experimental embryos electroporated with dsRNA derived from Endoglycan at HH21.
source: When the floor-plate morphology was analyzed at HH21, there was no difference between control (M-O) and experimental embryos electroporated with dsRNA derived from Endoglycan (P-R).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3M-R.

claim: There was no significant difference in spinal cord width at HH25 between untreated controls, EGFP-expressing controls, and dsEndo embryos.
source: There was no significant difference in spinal cord width at HH25 (400.2 ± 54.5 µm in untreated controls, 438.2 ± 30.3 µm in EGFP-expressing controls, and 394 ± 12.0 µm in dsEndo embryos), but floor plates were significantly narrower in embryos lacking Endoglycan (T; 61.6 ± 2.9 µm; n = 7 embryos; p<0.001) compared to untreated (82.4 ± 1.8 µm; n = 6 embryos) and EGFP-injected control embryos (83.6 ± 2.6 µm; n = 6 embryos).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: Floor plates were significantly narrower in embryos lacking Endoglycan (61.6 ± 2.9 µm) compared to untreated (82.4 ± 1.8 µm) and EGFP-injected control embryos (83.6 ± 2.6 µm) at HH25.
source: There was no significant difference in spinal cord width at HH25 (400.2 ± 54.5 µm in untreated controls, 438.2 ± 30.3 µm in EGFP-expressing controls, and 394 ± 12.0 µm in dsEndo embryos), but floor plates were significantly narrower in embryos lacking Endoglycan (T; 61.6 ± 2.9 µm; n = 7 embryos; p<0.001) compared to untreated (82.4 ± 1.8 µm; n = 6 embryos) and EGFP-injected control embryos (83.6 ± 2.6 µm; n = 6 embryos).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3T.

claim: The width of the floor plate was not different between groups when measured at HH21.
source: The width of the floor plate was not different between groups when measured at HH21 (V) with 70.1 ± 4.2 µm (n = 3) for untreated and 70.6 ± 2.5 µm for EGFP controls (n = 4), compared to 71.8 ± 2.0 µm for experimental embryos (n = 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3V.

claim: No changes in the expression of Contactin2 (Axonin-1) or NrCAM were found after silencing or overexpression of Endoglycan.
source: To exclude that the changes in axonal pathfinding seen after silencing or overexpression of Endoglycan were explained by an effect on the expression of known axon guidance cues for dI1 axons, Axonin-1/Contactin-2 (A–F) or NrCAM (G–L), we compared sections taken from control embryos electroporated with a plasmid encoding EGFP (A,D,G,J), embryos electroporated with dsEndo (B,E,H,K), or embryos overexpressing Endoglycan (C,F,I,L). We found no differences in expression of Axonin-1 and NrCAM.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: No changes in the expression of Shh or Wnt5a were found after silencing or overexpression of Endoglycan.
source: We did not find any changes in the expression of Shh (A–F) or Wnt5a (G–L) compared to control embryos expressing EGFP (A,D,G,J) after silencing Endoglycan (B,E,H,K) or after overexpression of Endoglycan (C,F,I,L).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Rescue of the aberrant axon guidance phenotype was only possible with specific concentrations of the Endoglycan plasmid: the medium concentration of the Endoglycan plasmid driven by the Hoxa1 promoter and the low concentration of the plasmid driven by the Math1 promoter.
source: In both cases, rescue was only possible with one concentration: the medium concentration of the Endoglycan plasmid driven by the Hoxa1 promoter and the low concentration of the plasmid driven by the Math1 promoter.
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: The amount, but not the source of Endoglycan matters for rescue of the axon guidance phenotype.
source: Because expression of these plasmids in control embryos (overexpression) resulted in aberrant behavior of axons at the floor plate, we used three different concentrations of plasmid for our rescue experiments and obtained a dose-dependent effect on axon guidance. Expression of high doses of Endoglycan was never able to rescue the axon guidance phenotype. However, axon guidance was not different from control embryos after transfection of dI1 neurons with a low concentration, or after transfection of floor-plate cells with a medium concentration of the Endoglycan ORF (Figure 4B; Table 1). Interestingly, the source of Endoglycan did not matter, but the amount of Endoglycan did.
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: Endoglycan did not act as a receptor.
source: Furthermore, these results suggested that Endoglycan did not act as a receptor.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiment data showing that the source of Endoglycan did not matter.

claim: Expression of Endoglycan reduced the number of commissural neurons on Endoglycan-expressing HEK cells compared to control HEK cells.
source: Expression of Endoglycan reduced the number of commissural neurons on Endoglycan-expressing HEK cells compared to control HEK cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The 'anti-adhesive' properties of Endoglycan depended on its post-translational modification.
source: These suggested 'anti-adhesive' properties of Endoglycan depended on its post-translational modification (Figure 5B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5B,D.

claim: Enzymatic removal of sialic acid by Neuraminidase or of O-linked glycans by O-glycosidase abolished the 'anti-adhesive' properties of Endoglycan expressed in HEK cells.
source: Enzymatic removal of sialic acid by Neuraminidase or of O-linked glycans by O-glycosidase abolished the 'anti-adhesive' properties of Endoglycan expressed in HEK cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Endoglycan had a similar effect on the adhesion of motoneurons to a layer of HEK cells expressing Endoglycan that also depended on the post-translational modification of Endoglycan with O-glycosylation and sialylation.
source: Endoglycan had a similar effect on the adhesion of motoneurons to a layer of HEK cells expressing Endoglycan that also depended on the post-translational modification of Endoglycan with O-glycosylation and sialylation (Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: It took only about half the time to detach commissural growth cones from HEK cells expressing Endoglycan compared to control HEK cells.
source: On average, it took only about half the time to detach commissural growth cones from HEK cells expressing Endoglycan compared to control HEK cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth cone blasting assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Overexpression of Endoglycan in neurons growing on control HEK cells significantly decreased the time it took to blast off growth cones compared to control neurons.
source: In line with this difference, overexpression of Endoglycan in neurons growing on control HEK cells significantly decreased the time it took to blast off growth cones compared to control neurons (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth cone blasting assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The difference in adhesive strength was not explained or markedly affected by differences in adhesive area between growth cones and HEK cells, as the growth cone areas did not differ between control and experimental conditions.
source: The difference in adhesive strength was not explained or markedly affected by differences in adhesive area between growth cones and HEK cells, as the growth cone areas did not differ between control and experimental conditions (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth cone area measurements shown in Figure 7.

claim: Endoglycan negatively regulated the adhesive strength between commissural growth cones and the HEK cells no matter whether Endoglycan was expressed in the growth cone or in the HEK cells.
source: Taken together, our in vitro experiments demonstrated that Endoglycan negatively regulated the adhesive strength between commissural growth cones and the HEK cells no matter whether Endoglycan was expressed in the growth cone or in the HEK cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro adhesion and growth cone blasting assay data shown in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: Commissural axons fail to enter the floor plate and turn prematurely along the ipsilateral floor-plate border in the absence of NrCAM.
source: Commissural axons cross the midline because of the positive signals provided by the interaction of floor-plate NrCAM with growth cone Contactin2 (Stoeckli and Landmesser, 1995; Stoeckli et al., 1997; Fitzli et al., 2000). In the absence of NrCAM or Contactin2, commissural axons fail to enter the floor plate and turn into the longitudinal axis prematurely along the ipsilateral floor-plate border.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Stoeckli and Landmesser, 1995; Stoeckli et al., 1997; Fitzli et al., 2000) and experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Concomitant downregulation of NrCAM and Endoglycan rescued the NrCAM phenotype.
source: This is indeed what we observed (Figure 8). As found previously (Stoeckli and Landmesser, 1995; Pekarik et al., 2003), axons were frequently turning prematurely along the ipsilateral floor-plate border in the absence of NrCAM (Figure 8A). In accordance with our hypothesis, ipsilateral turns were reduced to control levels when NrCAM and Endoglycan were downregulated concomitantly (Figure 8B,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Concomitant downregulation of NrCAM with Podocalyxin or CD34 had no effect on ipsilateral turns.
source: The rescue of the NrCAM phenotype was only seen for Endoglycan, as concomitant downregulation of NrCAM with Podocalyxin or CD34 had no effect on ipsilateral turns (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Growth cone speed in the first half of the floor plate was markedly slowed down to only 13 µm/hr after electroporation with dsRNA derived from Endoglycan.
source: In contrast, growth cone speed in the first half of the floor plate that was electroporated with dsRNA derived from Endoglycan (dsEndo) was markedly slowed down to only 13 µm/hr.
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data and kymograph analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: In the second, non-electroporated half of the floor plate, axons electroporated with dsEndo were faster than control axons (44 µm/hr).
source: In the second, non-electroporated half of the floor plate, axons electroporated with dsEndo were faster than control axons (44 µm/hr; E2).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data and kymograph analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: Axons overexpressing Endoglycan were faster in both halves of the floor plate (50 µm/hr).
source: Axons overexpressing Endoglycan were faster in both halves of the floor plate (50 µm/hr; F2).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data and kymograph analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: TdTomato-positive axons in control-injected spinal cords crossed the floor plate at a steady speed of 26 µm/h.
source: TdTomato-positive axons in control-injected spinal cords (D1-3) crossed the floor plate at a steady speed of 26 µm/h (D2) and turned rostrally in a highly organized manner (D3).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data and kymograph analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: Overexpression of Endoglycan significantly decreased the time axons needed to cross the entire floor plate compared to control and dsEndo conditions.
source: (B) Overexpression of Endoglycan significantly decreased the time axons needed to cross the entire floor plate compared to control and dsEndo conditions (Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's multiple-comparisons test).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of live imaging data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: There was a highly significant difference in the spinal cords unilaterally electroporated with dsEndo, as axons spent much longer in the first compared to the second half of the floor plate.
source: (C) The average time of crossing the first half and the second half of the floor plate was compared. Interestingly, there was a highly significant difference in the spinal cords unilaterally electroporated with dsEndo, as axons spent much longer in the first compared to the second half of the floor plate.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of live imaging data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Unilateral knockdown of Endoglycan resulted in a significant increase of the ratio of time spent in the first half of the floor plate and a decrease in the second half compared to both control and overexpression conditions.
source: (D) and (E) The ratios of the time axons spent in the first half (D) or the second half (E) of the floor plate divided by the time they needed to cross it entirely were compared between conditions. Unilateral knockdown of Endoglycan resulted in a significant increase of the ratio in the first half and a decrease in the second half compared to both control and overexpression conditions (one-way ANOVA with Sidak's multiple-comparisons test).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of live imaging data shown in Figure 10D,E.

claim: Overexpression of Endoglycan induced a significant reduction in the average growth cone area compared to the control condition in the first half of the floor plate.
source: (F) Overexpression of Endoglycan induced a significant reduction in the average growth cone area compared to the control condition (Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's multiple-comparisons test) but not compared to Endoglycan knockdown (p value = 0.08).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of live imaging data shown in Figure 10F.

claim: In the second half of the floor plate, the average growth cone area was reduced in both Endoglycan knockdown and overexpression condition compared to control.
source: (G) In the second half of the floor plate, the average growth cone area was reduced in both Endoglycan knockdown and overexpression condition compared to control (one-way ANOVA with Sidak's multiple-comparisons test).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of live imaging data shown in Figure 10G.

claim: At the floor-plate exit site, overexpression of Endoglycan induced a significant decrease in the average growth cone area compared to both control and knockdown conditions.
source: (H) At the floor-plate exit site, overexpression of Endoglycan induced a significant decrease in the average growth cone area compared to both control and knockdown conditions (one-way ANOVA with Sidak's multiple-comparisons test).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of live imaging data shown in Figure 10H.

claim: The average area of growth cones in the floor plate in control spinal cords was 50 ± 13 µm2 in the first, and 47 ± 12 µm2 in the second half of the floor plate.
source: The average area of growth cones in the floor plate in control spinal cords was 50 ± 13 µm2 in the first, and 47 ± 12 µm2 in the second half of the floor plate (Figure 11A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of live imaging data shown in Figure 11A.

claim: The growth cone area significantly increased at the floor-plate exit site, where growth cones need to choose to grow rostrally rather than caudally.
source: The growth cone area significantly increased at the floor-plate exit site, where growth cones need to choose to grow rostrally rather than caudally (Figure 11A). At the exit site, growth cone area was 106 ± 29 µm2 in control embryos.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of live imaging data shown in Figure 11A.

claim: Growth cones were significantly smaller in the first (43.5 ± 15 µm2) and the second half (41 ± 11 µm2) of the floor plate, as well as at the exit site (88 ± 28 µm2) in embryos overexpressing Endoglycan compared to controls.
source: In agreement with their faster speed in the floor plate overexpressing Endoglycan, growth cones were significantly smaller in the first (43.5 ± 15 µm2) and the second half (41 ± 11 µm2) of the floor plate, as well as at the exit site (88 ± 28 µm2) compared to controls (Figure 10F–H and Figure 11C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of live imaging data shown in Figures 10F-H and 11C.

claim: The tortuous, 'corkscrew'-like phenotype of axons was seen exclusively in spinal cords after knockdown of Endoglycan.
source: The tortuous, 'corkscrew'-like phenotype of axons was seen exclusively in spinal cords after knockdown of Endoglycan (Figure 12 and Videos 5 and 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 12 and Videos 5 and 6.

claim: Roundish EGFP-f-positive cells obstructed the smooth trajectory of dI1 axons in the commissure after knockdown of Endoglycan.
source: We could observe roundish EGFP-f-positive cells (arrows) that obstructed the smooth trajectory of dI1 axons in the commissure (arrowheads in Figure 12A1-5 and Video 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 12A1-5 and Video 5.

claim: dI1 axons were found to form loops in the layer where floor-plate cell somata were localized after knockdown of Endoglycan.
source: Moreover, dI1 axons were found to form loops in the layer where floor-plate cell somata were localized (arrowhead in Figure 12B1-5 and Video 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 12B1-5 and Video 6.

claim: Clusters of roundish EGFP-f-positive cells in the commissure were apparently causing axons to deviate from their trajectory by strongly adhering to them after knockdown of Endoglycan.
source: In the first half of the floor plate electroporated with dsEndo, clusters of roundish EGFP-f-positive cells in the commissure (arrows) were apparently causing axons to deviate from their trajectory by strongly adhering to them (arrowheads in Figure 12C1-5 and Video 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 12C1-5 and Video 6.

claim: Aberrant behavior of axons was only observed after many dI1 axons had already crossed the floor plate (after at least 10 hr).
source: We never found such aberrant behavior in control embryos or in embryos overexpressing Endoglycan. Moreover, we only observed these events after many dI1 axons had already crossed the floor plate (after at least 10 hr), supporting the hypothesis that the phenotype was due to excessive growth cone-floor plate adhesion resulting in floor-plate cell displacement.
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data and observations described in the manuscript.

claim: Endoglycan regulates migratory speed of growth cones by modulating their adhesion to floor-plate cells.
source: Furthermore, these observations suggest that Endoglycan regulates migratory speed of growth cones by modulating their adhesion to floor-plate cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the live imaging data and observations described in the manuscript.

claim: Axon-axon interactions did not seem to be different in the presence and absence of Endoglycan, as no effect on pre-crossing axons was found after perturbation of Endoglycan levels.
source: Taken together, our live imaging studies support results from in vitro adhesion experiments indicating that the level of Endoglycan expression modulates adhesive strength between dI1 commissural growth cones and floor-plate cells. In contrast, axon-axon interactions did not seem to be different in the presence and absence of Endoglycan, as we did not find any effect on pre-crossing axons after perturbation of Endoglycan levels (Figure 13).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 13.

claim: Endoglycan plays a vital role in commissural axon guidance at the ventral midline.
source: In summary, our results demonstrate a vital role for Endoglycan in commissural axon guidance at the ventral midline.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined in vivo and in vitro experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The observed phenotype is consistent with the hypothesis that Endoglycan is an essential regulator of cell-cell contacts by modulating the strength of adhesion between commissural axon growth cones and floor-plate cells.
source: The observed phenotype is consistent with the hypothesis that Endoglycan is an essential regulator of cell-cell contacts by modulating the strength of adhesion between commissural axon growth cones and floor-plate cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined in vivo and in vitro experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Neuronal attachment was negatively affected by the presence of an excess of Endoglycan in a glycosylation-dependent manner.
source: Neuronal attachment was negatively affected by the presence of an excess of Endoglycan in a glycosylation-dependent manner, indicating that Endoglycan decreases adhesive strength during neural circuit assembly.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Endoglycan decreases adhesive strength during neural circuit assembly.
source: Neuronal attachment was negatively affected by the presence of an excess of Endoglycan in a glycosylation-dependent manner, indicating that Endoglycan decreases adhesive strength during neural circuit assembly.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the in vitro adhesion assay data and the overall findings of the study.

claim: The phenotypes obtained in in vivo experiments and in live imaging observations in intact spinal cords are consistent with an anti-adhesive role of Endoglycan.
source: The phenotypes obtained in our in vivo experiments and in live imaging observations in intact spinal cords are consistent with an anti-adhesive role of Endoglycan.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined in vivo and live imaging experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Endoglycan may act like a 'lubricant' modulating the motility of growth cones in the floor plate by lowering stickiness.
source: This is further supported by the reduced adhesion of growth cones in in vitro assays. Thus, Endoglycan may act like a 'lubricant' modulating the motility of growth cones in the floor plate by lowering stickiness.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Such a function is supported by the structural features of sialomucins.
source: Such a function is supported by the structural features of sialomucins.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about the structural features of sialomucins.

claim: The function of CD34 family members has not been characterized in detail.
source: The function of CD34 family members has not been characterized in detail, but all the results obtained so far are compatible with an anti-adhesive role (Nielsen and McNagny, 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to published literature (Nielsen and McNagny, 2008).

claim: All the results obtained so far on CD34 family members are compatible with an anti-adhesive role.
source: The function of CD34 family members has not been characterized in detail, but all the results obtained so far are compatible with an anti-adhesive role (Nielsen and McNagny, 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to published literature (Nielsen and McNagny, 2008).

claim: A very specific glycosylation pattern of CD34 and Endoglycan was implicated in the interaction with L-selectin in lymph node cells, the so-called high endothelial venules (HEVs).
source: One exception are reports from lymph node cells, the so-called high endothelial venules (HEVs), where a very specific glycosylation patterns was implicated in the interaction of CD34 and Endoglycan with L-selectin (Furness and McNagny, 2006).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to published literature (Furness and McNagny, 2006).

claim: Observations suggest that Endoglycan acts as an anti-adhesive rather than as adhesive factor.
source: However, in agreement with most published studies on the role of CD34 and Podocalyxin (for reviews see Furness and McNagny, 2006; Nielsen and McNagny, 2008 and Nielsen and McNagny, 2009), our observations suggest that Endoglycan acts as an anti-adhesive rather than as adhesive factor.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript and citations to published literature (Furness and McNagny, 2006; Nielsen and McNagny, 2008; Nielsen and McNagny, 2009).

claim: This model is supported by results from in vivo and in vitro experiments that confirm a negative effect of Endoglycan on cell-cell adhesion.
source: This model is supported by results from in vivo and in vitro experiments that confirm a negative effect of Endoglycan on cell-cell adhesion (Figure 14).
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined in vivo and in vitro experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The adhesion-modulating effect of Endoglycan is mediated by the negatively charged mucin domain.
source: The adhesion-modulating effect of Endoglycan is mediated by the negatively charged mucin domain.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that enzymatic removal of sialic acid or O-linked glycans abolished the anti-adhesive properties of Endoglycan.

claim: Endoglycan could lower cell-cell adhesion by increasing the distance between adjacent cell membranes due to repulsion caused by the bulky, negatively charged posttranslational modifications of its extracellular domains.
source: Similar to the role suggested for the polysialic acid modification of NCAM (Rutishauser, 2008; Brusés and Rutishauser, 2001; Burgess et al., 2008), Endoglycan could lower cell-cell adhesion by increasing the distance between adjacent cell membranes due to repulsion caused by the bulky, negatively charged posttranslational modifications of its extracellular domains.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation based on the similarity to PSA-NCAM and is supported by citations to published literature (Rutishauser, 2008; Brusés and Rutishauser, 2001; Burgess et al., 2008).

claim: A similar effect was found for PSA-NCAM in hindlimb innervation.
source: A similar effect was found for PSA-NCAM in hindlimb innervation (Tang et al., 1994; Landmesser et al., 1990) and in the visual system, where retinal ganglion cell axons innervating the tectum were found to regulate axon-axon adhesion versus axon-target cell adhesion (Rutishauser et al., 1988).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to published literature (Tang et al., 1994; Landmesser et al., 1990; Rutishauser et al., 1988).

claim: The same mechanism was found in motoneurons, where axon-axon versus axon-muscle fiber adhesion was a determining factor for the appropriate innervation pattern.
source: The same mechanism was found in motoneurons, where axon-axon versus axon-muscle fiber adhesion was a determining factor for the appropriate innervation pattern.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about PSA-NCAM function in motoneurons.

claim: In contrast to PSA-NCAM that continues to play a role in synaptic plasticity in the adult nervous system, the function of Endoglycan appears to be restricted to development.
source: In contrast to PSA-NCAM that continues to play a role in synaptic plasticity in the adult nervous system, the function of Endoglycan appears to be restricted to development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the expression pattern of Endoglycan and the comparison with PSA-NCAM.

claim: The mechanisms by which Endoglycan reduces adhesion of growth cones and floor-plate cells might be similar to PSA-NCAM.
source: Our findings together with structural features of Endoglycan suggest that the mechanisms by which Endoglycan reduces adhesion of growth cones and floor-plate cells might be similar.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation based on the similarity to PSA-NCAM.

claim: Additional studies will be required to verify whether the effect of Endoglycan as modulator of adhesive strength uses the exact same mechanism as PSA-NCAM.
source: Additional studies will be required to verify whether the effect of Endoglycan as modulator of adhesive strength uses the exact same mechanism as PSA-NCAM.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the need for future research.

claim: Commissural axons crossing the floor plate are suggested to do so by close interaction with short filopodial processes of floor-plate cells.
source: Commissural axons crossing the floor plate are suggested to do so by close interaction with short filopodial processes of floor-plate cells (Dumoulin et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to published literature (Dumoulin et al., 2021).

claim: The aberrant morphology of the floor plate at HH25 could be explained by the inability of axons to break contacts with floor-plate cells in the absence of Endoglycan.
source: Thus, the aberrant morphology of the floor plate at HH25 could be explained by the inability of axons to break contacts with floor-plate cells in the absence of Endoglycan, consistent with our hypothesis that Endoglycan is a negative regulator of adhesion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data and is consistent with the hypothesis.

claim: The perturbation of the balance in growth cone-floor plate adhesion led to impaired timing of midline crossing.
source: Live imaging data demonstrated that the perturbation of the balance in growth cone-floor plate adhesion led to impaired timing of midline crossing, which in turn might also interfere with the correct sensing and reading of guidance cues by dI1 growth cones, and prevented them from making the correct decision at the floor-plate exit site (Figures 9 and 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figures 9 and 10.

claim: Impaired timing of midline crossing might interfere with the correct sensing and reading of guidance cues by dI1 growth cones.
source: Live imaging data demonstrated that the perturbation of the balance in growth cone-floor plate adhesion led to impaired timing of midline crossing, which in turn might also interfere with the correct sensing and reading of guidance cues by dI1 growth cones, and prevented them from making the correct decision at the floor-plate exit site (Figures 9 and 10).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the live imaging data.

claim: Impaired timing of midline crossing prevented dI1 growth cones from making the correct decision at the floor-plate exit site.
source: Live imaging data demonstrated that the perturbation of the balance in growth cone-floor plate adhesion led to impaired timing of midline crossing, which in turn might also interfere with the correct sensing and reading of guidance cues by dI1 growth cones, and prevented them from making the correct decision at the floor-plate exit site (Figures 9 and 10).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the live imaging data shown in Figures 9 and 10.

claim: Endoglycan affects neural circuit formation by modulating the interaction of many different guidance cues and their surface receptors.
source: Rather than acting as a guidance cue or guidance receptor, we suggest that Endoglycan affects neural circuit formation by modulating the interaction of many different guidance cues and their surface receptors.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Endoglycan acts as an 'anti-adhesive' factor in axon guidance that is fine-tuning the balance between adhesion and de-adhesion.
source: In summary, we propose an 'anti-adhesive' role for Endoglycan in axon guidance that is fine-tuning the balance between adhesion and de-adhesion (Figure 14).
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined in vivo and in vitro experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Precise regulation of cell-cell contacts is required in both cell migration and axonal pathfinding processes.
source: Precise regulation of cell-cell contacts is required in both processes and is fundamental for developmental processes that depend on a high degree of plasticity and a plethora of specific molecular interactions.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about developmental processes.

claim: Precise regulation of cell-cell contacts is fundamental for developmental processes that depend on a high degree of plasticity and a plethora of specific molecular interactions.
source: Precise regulation of cell-cell contacts is required in both processes and is fundamental for developmental processes that depend on a high degree of plasticity and a plethora of specific molecular interactions.
